metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work report, claude-hai channel. Episode 8, from the last pushed commit on feat/snickerdoodle-cli (d85106b; origin contains it and the branch is in sync). FRAMEWORK: three questions for any percentage — WHAT IS THE DENOMINATOR / COULD EVERY ITEM HAVE BEEN FOUND / IS THE SHARE ONE DEFECT OR MANY. Hero beat is B05: one numerator over three denominators giving 4%, 200% and 100%, where the impossible middle answer is the only reason the plausible first one was caught. Every figure reproduced by running the committed checker read-only; the 97-vs-99 discrepancy against episode 7 is reconciled on screen. See FACTCHECK.md.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane, and this is my week on Mycroft. I built a checker, and it told me a defect affected four percent of the repository. That number was wrong, and the thing that caught it was a second number that came out at two hundred percent.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the week's ask, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the week's ask and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "how widespread are the recipe/script contract mismatches? give me a number"

beats.role_note: series continuity — episode 7 made the checker read the code; this week asks what the code promised
beats.narration_text: Last episode I made the conformance checker actually open the step scripts. This week goes one layer up. Every recipe in the repository ends by telling the reader to run a command called snickerdoodle. That command had never existed. The instruction was written one thousand four hundred and forty-four times across ninety-seven recipes, and nobody could run it.
beats.new_visual_element: the spec that was written 1444 times and never built

shot.show: the documented command, the count, and the fact that it did not exist
shot.visual_intent: A bordered card holds the documented command in monospace. Beneath it, two stat cards: 1444 occurrences, 97 recipes. A terracotta strike crosses the connector between the command card and a small card reading 'never existed'.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions for any percentage, shown AS A STRUCTURE before the numbers
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any percentage in any report. One: what is the denominator — name the population out loud. Two: could every item in it actually have been found — or are some of them sitting in the denominator as silent passes. Three: is the share one defect or many — because a finding in ninety-seven percent of things that share a template is one defect, not ninety-four.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: WHAT IS THE DENOMINATOR / COULD EVERY ITEM BE FOUND / ONE DEFECT OR MANY
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The second lands in terracotta — it is the question this episode turns on — and the rest of the reel is scored against all three.

beats.narration_text: The ask was simple. Stop finding these one at a time by failing on them, and measure how widespread they are without running anything.

shot.show: the composer with the check ask

props.command: claude "compare what each recipe documents against what its scripts implement — without executing them"
props.segment: The ask · measure it, do not run it
output: 582 scripts is a lot of subprocesses
running a file to learn its flags is a side effect

beats.role_note: what check found — reproduced by running the committed checker
beats.narration_text: Here is what it found. Ninety-seven recipes, six hundred and sixteen findings. Ninety-four of the ninety-seven name step scripts that do not exist on disk. And the number that matters for what comes next: zero recipes came back clean.

shot.visual_intent: Three bordered stat cards across the top — 97, 616, 94 of 97 — then a fourth beneath in terracotta reading 0 clean. The citation strip names the committed checker and the command used to reproduce it.

beats.role_note: THE HERO BEAT — three denominators for one numerator, and only one of them is right
beats.narration_text: Now the denominator. Four recipes advertise a flag that no script implements. Score that against all ninety-seven and you get four percent, which reads as rare. But ninety-three of those ninety-seven have no scripts on disk at all — they could never have produced this finding. They were sitting in the denominator as silent passes. Second attempt: score it against recipes with no missing scripts. That is two. Four over two. Two hundred percent. The right denominator is recipes with at least one script to compare — four. Four over four. One hundred percent. Not rare. Universal.
beats.new_visual_element: the same numerator over three different denominators

shot.visual_intent: Three rows, each a bordered card: numerator over denominator on the left, the resulting percentage large on the right, and a verdict chip. Row one in soft ink reads 'plausible, wrong'. Row two in terracotta reads 'impossible, and therefore useful'. Row three in ink reads 'right'. The citation strip names the checker's own summary.

beats.role_note: ACTUAL-CODE LAW — the comment the source carries about its own denominator
beats.narration_text: The checker says this out loud in its own source. The comment records why the obvious denominator is wrong: scoring the findings out of all ninety-seven reports them as rare when they are near universal among the recipes where they are measurable at all.
beats.new_visual_element: the source's own note on the denominator

shot.show: the denominator comment, verbatim from the committed file

props.title: scripts/snickerdoodle.mjs  @ d85106b
props.sparkLine: The denominator is part of the finding

beats.role_note: question 3 — a share is not a count when the population shares a template
beats.narration_text: Question three, and it changes what you do on Monday. Ninety-four recipes name scripts that do not exist. That is not ninety-four defects. They all inherit the same template, so it is one defect, in one place, repeated ninety-four times. Read as ninety-four, it is a quarter's work. Read as one, it is an afternoon — and fixing it there closes it everywhere.

shot.show: 94 independent defects vs one template defect inherited 94 times
shot.visual_intent: Left: a scatter of ninety-four small hollow squares, read as independent, labelled 'a quarter's work'. Right: one terracotta square at the top with connectors fanning down to the same ninety-four, labelled 'one defect, inherited'. A short connector runs between the two readings.

beats.role_note: the recount — every figure reproduced, and the 97-vs-99 reconciled
beats.narration_text: The series rule is to recount rather than trust the commit message, so I ran the committed checker myself. Ninety-seven recipes, six hundred and sixteen findings, ninety-four of ninety-seven, four of four at a hundred percent — every figure reproduces exactly. And one discrepancy resolved rather than found: last episode I counted ninety-nine recipes, this one says ninety-seven. There are ninety-nine files. Ninety-seven of them carry the snickerdoodle contract. Both numbers were right; they were counting different things.
beats.new_visual_element: five figures reproduced, and the 99/97 reconciliation

shot.show: 97 / 616 / 94 / 4-of-4 reproduced; then 99 files vs 97 with the contract
shot.visual_intent: Four rows with drawn ticks and the reproduced values. Beneath, a bordered terracotta panel reconciling 99 files against 97 carrying the contract, with 1444 occurrences cited. The strip names the command that was run.

beats.role_note: the companion commit — the CLI itself, and the bug that would have recorded a false failure
beats.narration_text: The other commit built the command. It was extracted, not invented — the spec was already written in every recipe. Gate decisions now refuse an approval when the gate's own test fails, refuse any decision without a note, and require a named human. Approving anything that touches live action takes a second deliberate flag. And one bug worth the whole commit: gate tests are POSIX shell, but on Windows they were running under the wrong shell, so a gate reported a failure for a test that actually passes. That would have been written down as real evidence.
beats.new_visual_element: what the CLI refuses, and the false-failure bug

shot.show: the gate's four refusals, then the shell bug that faked a failure
shot.visual_intent: Left: a bordered panel listing the four refusals as monospace rows. Right: a terracotta panel showing the shell mismatch and its consequence — a passing test recorded as a failure. The citation strip names the companion commit.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric on the viewer's own metrics, with a GOOD/BAD discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Find a percentage in your own dashboard and ask what is in its denominator. Then ask how many of those could actually have failed. If something cannot produce the finding, it is not a pass — it is not a measurement at all.

shot.show: the composer with the handoff prompt and a GOOD/BAD discriminator
